story.lead: Broken street lights top BBMP complaints
story.summary: BBMP grievance records published on OpenCity show that one problem towers over the rest: street lights that don't work. Of all complaints filed from February 2020 to June 2025, **293,580** were about street lights. That is more than the next three complaint types put together (garbage vehicle not arrived, garbage dump and potholes). Below, we look at which departments get the most complaints, which specific problems lead, and how street light complaints changed by year.
story.sub: BBMP grievance records, complaints filed 8 February 2020 to 19 June 2025; yearly view covers 2021 to 2024.

facts.label: complaints about street lights not working
complaints to the Electrical department
street light complaints filed in 2024

points.h: Three departments get most of the complaints
points.p: Start with the departments. Electrical is far ahead with **310,128** complaints. Garbage-related complaints come next at **195,153**, and road maintenance follows with **111,535**. After that the numbers drop sharply: Forest, the fourth, has **34,618**, less than a third of road maintenance. Everyday services like light, rubbish and roads make up the bulk of what people report.

points.h: One complaint stands out: lights that don't work
points.p: Zooming in on specific problems makes the picture sharper. **Street Light Not Working** alone has **293,580** complaints, which is almost all of the Electrical department's total. Garbage is split into two big problems: **73,108** said the garbage vehicle did not arrive, and **66,680** reported a garbage dump. Potholes come fourth with **32,655**. Street lights get about four times as many complaints as the next single problem.

points.h: Street light complaints rose sharply in 2024
points.p: Has this been a steady problem? Looking only at the complete years 2021 to 2024, street light complaints stayed between **47,641** and **53,848** for three years. Then 2024 jumped to **71,430**. That is about 46% more than in 2023. These are complaints filed through BBMP's system, so the rise shows more filings, not necessarily more broken lights.

story.takeaway: People complain to BBMP most about street lights, then garbage collection, then roads and potholes. Across the whole period, street lights lead by a wide margin. The figures count complaints filed, not how many problems exist.
story.note: Counts are complaints filed, and 2020 and 2025 are partial years, so only 2021 to 2024 are compared year by year.

story.lead: Thanisandra filed the most garbage complaints.
story.summary: BBMP grievance records published on OpenCity show Thanisandra, in north-east Bengaluru, filed **5,553** garbage complaints between February 2020 and June 2025. That is the most of any of the city's 198 old wards. Rajarajeshwari Nagar (**5,143**) and Someshwara (**4,712**) follow close behind. Below, we look at the top 15, whether 2024 tells the same story, and how the yearly total changed.

Jnanabharathi Ward (4,679) and Horamavu (4,069) complete the top five. The 15th ward, Hoodi, has 2,478, less than half of Thanisandra's count, so the counts fall off steadily down the list. points.h: In 2024 alone, Doddanekkundi moves to the top
points.p: Looking at just 2024, the order changes a little. Doddanekkundi leads with **1,492** complaints, while Thanisandra drops to second with **1,404**. Someshwara, Gottigere and Horamavu follow. Rajarajeshwari Nagar falls from second overall to tenth, with 1,030. Kumaraswamy Layout (977) and Vishwanathnagenahalli (879) appear in the top 15 for 2024 but not in the whole-period list. So the top of the list shifts from year to year.

points.h: Complaints filed doubled in 2024

In 2024 they jumped to **57,329**, about twice the 2023 figure. This is a count of complaints filed, not proof that garbage problems doubled. It also helps explain why 2024 gives each top ward a large share of its total: Doddanekkundi's 1,492 in 2024 alone is nearly half its five-year level of 3,126.

story.takeaway: Thanisandra, Rajarajeshwari Nagar and Someshwara have filed the most garbage complaints overall. In 2024 Doddanekkundi took the top spot. Because filings roughly doubled in 2024, the ranking mixes real ward differences with more complaints being filed.

story.lead: Streetlight complaints jumped in 2024 after three flat years
story.summary: BBMP grievance records published on OpenCity show that "Street Light Not Working" is the single biggest kind of complaint in Bengaluru. For three years the yearly count stayed between about 48,000 and 54,000. In 2024 it shot up to **71,430** complaints filed, about 46% more than 2023's **48,991**. Below, we look at the yearly totals, the month-by-month climb, and how much of all complaints this one problem makes up.
story.sub: BBMP grievance records on OpenCity, 2021 to 2024 (complete years) and monthly to May 2025.

facts.label: streetlight complaints filed in 2024
filed in May 2025, the highest month shown
share of all complaints in 2024, down from 46%

points.h: Three steady years, then a big jump
points.p: Start with the yearly totals. Complaints filed were **47,641** in 2021, **53,848** in 2022 and **48,991** in 2023, so they moved up and down within a narrow range. Then 2024 reached **71,430**. That is about 22,000 more than the year before. These are complaints filed through BBMP's system, so they show how many people complained, not necessarily how many lights failed.

points.h: The climb was gradual, not a single spike
points.p: The monthly figures show how the jump happened. In early 2023 the city saw about 2,400 to 3,100 complaints a month, and by mid-2023 it was near 5,000. In 2024 it started at about 4,400 in January, rose to **7,585** in October and stayed above 7,000 through December. The level did not fall back in 2025: every month from January to May was above 5,800, and May 2025 hit **8,289**. The higher level (above 5,800 a month since May 2024) has lasted about a year.

points.h: Streetlights are a smaller slice of a growing pile
points.p: Streetlights are still the biggest single complaint, but their share is falling. They were **46%** of all complaints in 2021 and **34.5%** in 2024. That does not mean fewer streetlight complaints, since the count rose. It means other kinds of complaints grew even faster in 2024. Streetlights remain about one in three complaints filed.

story.takeaway: Streetlight complaints were steady until 2023, then rose sharply through 2024 and stayed high into 2025. Their share of all complaints fell because the total grew faster. The figures count complaints filed, not broken lights.
story.note: Complaints jumped overall in 2024 because more were filed through BBMP's system, which is not proof that problems doubled; 2025 data ends in June.

story.lead: Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam won the most seats
story.summary: Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) came first in the May 2026 Tamil Nadu election, with **108** of the 234 seats. That is almost twice as many as the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), which won **59**. The 108 seats are short of the 118 needed for a majority on their own, if you count a majority as more than half of 234. Below, we look at seats, votes and the very closest contests.
story.sub: Tamil Nadu Assembly election results, May 2026, as republished on OpenCity: all 234 constituencies.

facts.label: seats won by TVK
TVK's share of all votes statewide
winning margin in Tiruppattur, the closest seat

points.h: TVK leads, with DMK and AIADMK behind
points.p: Election results published on OpenCity show TVK won **108** seats. The DMK came second with **59**, and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) third with **47**. Together those three parties took 214 of the 234 seats. The other 20 seats were spread across a handful of smaller parties, with the Indian National Congress the largest on 5.

points.h: The vote share backs up the seat count
points.p: Seats are won constituency by constituency, so votes and seats can differ. Here they point the same way. TVK got **34.9%** of all votes statewide, against **24.2%** for the DMK and **21.2%** for the AIADMK. TVK's share is about 10.7 points higher than the DMK's. Naam Tamilar Katchi won no seats in the chart but took **4%** of the votes.

points.h: Some seats were decided by a handful of votes
points.p: Some contests were extremely tight. TVK won Tiruppattur from the DMK by just **1 vote**. The DMK won Veppanahalli by **138** votes, and the AIADMK won Kanniyakumari by **214**. Of the ten closest seats, TVK won three, the AIADMK four, the DMK two and the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi one. In every one of these ten seats the winner was ahead by fewer than 750 votes.

story.takeaway: TVK won the election clearly, with the most seats and the most votes. It was well ahead of the DMK and AIADMK on both counts. A few seats, though, were won by only a few votes.
story.note: The table lists results only, with no alliances, so this compares single parties and does not add up alliance totals.

story.lead: One seat in Tamil Nadu was won by one vote
story.summary: In Tamil Nadu's May 2026 assembly election, Tiruppattur was decided by a single vote. Results published on OpenCity show that six of the 234 seats were won by fewer than 500 votes. Fifteen seats were won by fewer than 1,000. Here is how thin those margins were, who won them, and how they compare with the rest of the state.
story.sub: Based on Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly election results, May 2026, all 234 constituencies.

facts.label: Winning margin in Tiruppattur, the closest seat
Seats won by fewer than 1,000 votes
Seats won by 10,000 votes or more

points.h: Tiruppattur was settled by one vote
points.p: Start with the 15 tightest seats. Tiruppattur tops the list with a margin of **1 vote**. Veppanahalli follows at **138 votes**, then Kanniyakumari at 214 and Polur at 227. The 15th seat on the list, Udhagamandalam, was still won by only 976 votes. In the closest of these seats, a few hundred votes at most separated the winner from the runner-up.

points.h: The close wins were spread across many parties
points.p: So who won these nail-biters? Among the 20 closest seats, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam won **7**, the most of any party. The All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam won **5** and the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam won 4. Four other parties won one each: the Indian Union Muslim League, the Bharatiya Janata Party, Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi and Pattali Makkal Katchi. No single party owned the close finishes.

points.h: Most seats were not close at all
points.p: Zoom out and the close seats are a small group. Only **6** seats had a margin under 500 votes, and 9 more fell between 500 and 999. At the other end, **130** of the 234 seats were won by 10,000 votes or more. That is 130 of 234, a little over half. Another 43 seats were won by 5,000 to 9,999 votes. The nail-biters were the exception, but they were close enough to matter.

story.takeaway: A handful of seats came down to a few hundred votes, and one came down to a single vote. Seven different parties shared the 20 closest wins. Even so, more than half of all seats were won comfortably.

story.lead: Chennai Metro ridership is growing about 6% a year
story.summary: Chennai Metro carried about **112 million** journeys in 2025, up from **105 million** in 2024. That is roughly **6.5%** more, or nearly 7 million extra trips. Figures published on OpenCity show the same steady climb in the first half of 2026. Below, we check the full years, then the same months side by side, then the month-by-month ride.
story.sub: Chennai Metro Rail monthly passenger totals, April 2023 to June 2026, as published on OpenCity.

facts.label: Growth in yearly riders, 2024 to 2025
Jan-Jun 2026 versus Jan-Jun 2025
Busiest month: July 2025

points.h: A full year brings 7 million more journeys
points.p: Start with the only two complete years in the data. Chennai Metro had **105.2 million** journeys in 2024 and **112.1 million** in 2025. That is about **6.5%** growth, or 6.9 million more trips. These count journeys, not separate people.

points.h: The first half of 2026 keeps the pace
points.p: Does the growth continue into this year? Comparing January to June in each year gives a fair test, because every year gets the same months. Riders went from **50.7 million** in 2024 to **53.5 million** in 2025, a rise of about 5.4%. In 2026 the total reached **56.7 million**, about 6.1% above 2025. points.h: Month by month, 2025 beat 2024 every time

Each of the nine 2025 months shown, January to September, was higher than the same month of 2024. July 2025 hit **10.47 million**, about 9.8% above July 2024. The rows shown here stop at September 2025, so they don't cover the 2026 months.

story.takeaway: Chennai Metro ridership is growing steadily, by about 6% a year. The yearly totals, the same-month comparison and the monthly figures all point the same way. Growth hasn't slowed in the first half of 2026.
story.note: Figures are journeys, not people, and 2024 and 2025 are the only complete years in the data.

story.lead: Chennai's reservoirs nearly ran dry in 2019
story.summary: In August 2019, the five reservoirs that supply Chennai held just **112 mcft** of water in total. That is about one twenty-fifth of what they held in January (**2,842 mcft**). Three of the five reservoirs hit zero at some point in the year. Here is how the year fell and then recovered. Mcft means million cubic feet, the unit the water figures are published in.
story.sub: Monthly reservoir storage published for Chennai's five drinking-water reservoirs, January to December 2019.

facts.label: Lowest total storage, August 2019
Reservoirs that fell to zero in 2019
Total storage by December 2019

points.h: Storage fell month after month, then bounced back
points.p: Across all five reservoirs, storage started 2019 at **2,842 mcft** and slid for most of the year. By June it was **818 mcft**, by July **377**, and in August it bottomed out at **112 mcft**. Then it turned fast: **1,267 mcft** in September and **4,817 mcft** by December. That December figure is well above where the year began.

points.h: Three reservoirs went completely empty
points.p: The total hides differences between reservoirs. Red Hills, Cholavaram and Chembarambakkam each hit **0 mcft** at their lowest point in 2019. Poondi was down to **16 mcft**. Only Veeranam, the reservoir far to the south that pipes water to the city, stayed well above that, with a low of **96 mcft**. So the shortage was really a crisis at the reservoirs closest to the city.

points.h: Near the city, almost nothing was left for months
points.p: Take Veeranam out and the picture is starker. The four nearby reservoirs held **1,389 mcft** in January and only **61 mcft** in June. They then sat at **18**, **16** and **16 mcft** in July, August and September. The recovery came in the last three months, with **713 mcft** in October, **2,789** in November and **3,473** in December. For about three months, these reservoirs held almost no water.

story.takeaway: Chennai's reservoirs fell to almost nothing in mid-2019. The four reservoirs near the city held only 16 mcft in August and September, and three of the five touched zero. They refilled quickly in the last months of the year.
story.note: The reservoir data ends in December 2021, so it says nothing about how full the reservoirs are today.

story.lead: Delhi and Mumbai are Bengaluru's busiest flight routes
story.summary: Two cities stand far above the rest of Bengaluru's domestic flight routes: Delhi and Mumbai. In 2023, the latest complete year, about **4.77 million** passengers flew between Bengaluru and Delhi, and **4.40 million** between Bengaluru and Mumbai, counting both directions. That is about twice the next route, Hyderabad, at 2.29 million. The charts below show the same pattern in 2023, over the whole 2015–2025 period, and in 2025 so far.

points.p: Start with 2023, the latest full year. Delhi came first with **4.77 million** passengers and Mumbai second with **4.40 million**, counting people flying in both directions. Hyderabad was third with **2.29 million**, less than half of Delhi's total. Kolkata, Pune, Kochi and Goa followed, each with between 1.58 and 1.85 million.

points.h: Over ten years, the same two cities stay on top
points.p: Zoom out to every month in the data and the order barely changes. story.lead: COVID cut Bengaluru's flight traffic by more than half
story.summary: In April 2020, no passengers were recorded on flights between Bengaluru and other Indian cities. Two months earlier, in February 2020, there were **2.36 million**. Over the whole of 2020, DGCA figures show **12.44 million** passengers, down from **28.73 million** in 2019. That is a fall of about 57%. The charts below show the yearly drop, the month-by-month collapse and slow climb back, and what happened to air freight.
story.sub: DGCA passenger and freight figures for routes to and from Bengaluru, complete years 2016–2020, 2022 and 2023, plus monthly figures from July 2019 to January 2022.

facts.label: fall in passengers, 2019 to 2020
passengers recorded in April 2020
passengers in 2023, above the 2019 level

points.h: A steady climb, then a cliff in 2020
points.p: Before COVID, traffic was rising every year. It grew from **18.59 million** passengers in 2016 to **28.73 million** in 2019. Then 2020 fell to **12.44 million**, about 16 million fewer than the year before. 2022 reached 24.37 million, still below 2019. By 2023 it hit **32.54 million**, about 13% above 2019. The drop was deep, but it did not last.

points.h: Traffic hit zero in April 2020, then crept back
points.p: The yearly total hides how sudden the fall was. Passengers were at 2.36 million in February 2020 and 1.42 million in March. In April the figure was 0, and in May just 0.07 million. From there the recovery was slow: 1.12 million in October 2020 and 1.46 million in December. Recovery was not smooth. The monthly figure fell back to 0.51 million in June 2021, the month after the one missing from the data. It reached 2.04 million in December 2021, close to the 2.53 million of December 2019.

points.h: Cargo fell too, but by much less
points.p: Air freight tells a similar story with a smaller drop. Freight on these routes went from **167,298** tonnes in 2019 to **117,699** in 2020, a fall of about 30%. That is far gentler than the 57% fall in passengers. Freight was back at 156,734 tonnes in 2022, still below 2019. In 2023 it reached **180,050** tonnes, about 8% above 2019. Cargo was hit, but it recovered to above its old level.

story.takeaway: COVID almost stopped flying to and from Bengaluru for a time. Passengers fell by more than half in 2020, and air freight fell by about 30%. Both were back above 2019 levels by 2023.
story.note: 2021 is left out of the yearly charts because the data has no figure for May 2021. Figures cover only routes between Bengaluru and Indian cities.

story.lead: Not wearing a helmet tops Bengaluru's traffic cases
story.summary: Bengaluru Traffic Police records published on OpenCity show that helmet offences are booked more than any other. In 2024, riders without a helmet led with **3.19 million** cases, and pillion riders (the passengers) without one added **2.10 million**. Together that is more than five times the cases for wrong parking, the next most common offence. The charts below show the 2024 list, how it changed in 2025, and the long run for riders without helmets.

points.h: Helmets dominate the 2024 list
points.p: Start with 2024, the latest year with the full list of offences. Riders without a helmet were booked **3,191,814** times, and pillion riders without one **2,097,153** times. Together that is about **5.29 million** cases, more than five times the **973,071** for wrong parking in third place. Jumping a signal (680,900) and driving without a seat belt (421,816) came next.

points.h: In 2025 the top still holds, but the gaps shrink
points.p: The 2025 list has the same offences at the top, but the order and sizes moved. points.h: Rider helmet cases rose for years, then fell
points.p: Zoom out and the helmet story has a clear arc. Cases for riders without a helmet grew from 1.65 million in 2018 to a peak of **4,392,381** in 2022. They have dropped every year since. The 2025 figure of **2,033,259** is less than half the peak, though still above the 2018 level. Even so, it remains the single most common offence on the 2025 list.

story.takeaway: Helmet offences are the most common traffic cases in Bengaluru, with riders without helmets at the top in both 2024 and 2025. Their numbers have fallen since 2022, while cases for wrong parking and missing seat belts rose from 2024 to 2025.
story.note: These are cases booked, which depend on how much enforcement and camera checking happens, not only on how people drive. The 2025 list covers fewer offences than 2024.

story.lead: Bengaluru's air is cleanest in July and the monsoon months.
story.summary: Bengaluru's air is cleanest in the middle of the year. July is the best month, with fine dust (PM2.5) averaging **18.7** micrograms per cubic metre across the city's stations. March is the dirtiest month at **42.9**, more than twice as high. The charts below show the same pattern in two kinds of dust and in how often the air crosses India's daily limit.

facts.label: Average PM2.5 in July, the cleanest month

points.h: Fine dust drops to its lowest from June to September
points.p: PM2.5 is fine dust that can get deep into the lungs. The average across Bengaluru's stations falls from **33.6** in April to **23.9** in May. It then stays low through the monsoon: **20.2** in June, **18.7** in July, **20.9** in August and **21.8** in September. After that it climbs again, reaching **39.5** in December. So the cleanest stretch runs from about May to September.

points.h: Coarser dust follows the same yearly curve
points.p: The pattern isn't a quirk of one measure. PM10, which covers larger dust particles, is also lowest in July at **49.8**. It is highest in January at **94.4** and in March at **93.5**. The months from June to September all stay under **57**, while December is at **82.8**. Both kinds of dust agree on which months are clean.

points.h: In the cleanest months, days over the limit almost vanish
points.p: India's 24-hour limit for PM2.5 is 60 micrograms per cubic metre. In July only **0.2%** of station-days went above it, and in September also **0.2%**. In January and December the share was **14%** and **13.9%**, roughly one in seven station-days. March was also high at **13.9%**. Monsoon air rarely crosses the limit, while winter and early spring often do.

story.takeaway: Bengaluru's air is cleanest from June to September, and July is the best month. It is worst in winter and in March. The monsoon months are the ones with almost no days above India's daily limit.
story.note: These are averages across Bengaluru's stations for 2024 and 2025 combined, so each calendar month has two years of readings, and the figures are not the official AQI.

story.lead: Pune's air broke the limit 695 times in 2025
story.summary: Pune's monitors recorded **695** station-days in 2025 when PM2.5, a fine dust that gets deep into the lungs, was above India's daily limit of 60 micrograms per cubic metre. A station-day is one monitor on one day, so one bad day can count several times. The problem swings hugely with the seasons: in December, **76.8%** of valid readings were above the limit, while in July and August none were. Below, we look at when it happened and which stations saw it most.

points.h: Winter months carry most of the bad days
points.p: Counting every monitor, the breaches pile up at the ends of the year. December was the worst month with **189** station-days above the limit, followed by January with **126**. November, January, February and December together hold 503 of the 695, about 72%. July and August had **0**, and September had just 1.

points.h: In December, three in four readings were over the limit
points.p: Raw counts can mislead, because monitors miss some days. So this chart shows the share of valid readings above 60. December tops it at **76.8%**, which means most monitor-days that month were over the limit. November was at 45.5% and January at 48.6%. The share fell to 0.9% in June and 0% in July and August, then climbed again from October (16%).

points.h: Some stations saw far more bad days than others
points.p: The breaches were not spread evenly across the city. Revenue Colony-Shivajinagar had the most, with **140** days above the limit, then Bhumkar Nagar with **122**. Together those two stations had 262 days. At the other end, Bhosari had **8**, so the top station had more than 17 times as many. This list only includes stations with at least 60 valid days, but stations have different numbers of valid days (some, like Dhankawadi, only began in 2025), so the counts are not strictly like for like.

story.takeaway: Pune's air went above India's daily PM2.5 limit mostly in winter, and it got worse towards the end of 2025. The monsoon months were almost clear. Where you live in the city also mattered a lot.
story.note: These are station-days against India's 24-hour PM2.5 standard of 60 µg/m³, not the official AQI, and Pune's stations have different numbers of valid days.

story.lead: Bengaluru's wettest year on record was 2022
story.summary: Rainfall figures for Bengaluru go back to 1901, and the wettest year in all that time is 2022, with **1,890 mm**. That is about 190 mm more than 2017, the second wettest at **1,696 mm**. Three of the ten wettest years have come since 2017. Below, we look at the top ten, the last 15 years, and how rain has changed decade by decade.
story.sub: Monthly rainfall for Bengaluru, 1901 to 2025, added up by calendar year.

facts.label: Rain in 2022, the wettest year since 1901
Average per year in the 2020s so far
Rain in 2018, the driest of the last 15 years

points.h: Recent years dominate the top ten
points.p: The ten wettest years put 2022 clearly in front at **1,890 mm**, followed by 2017 (**1,696 mm**) and 2021 (**1,511 mm**). The top three are all from the last nine years. Older wet years do appear: 1998, 1991, 1916, 1903 and 1958 all made the list. Even so, 2015 is the only other year from after 2005 in the top ten, so recent years hold four of the ten places.

points.h: The last 15 years swing between dry and soaking
points.p: Recent years have not been steadily wet. Rain fell as low as **618 mm** in 2018 and as high as **1,890 mm** in 2022. The three years from 2020 to 2022 rose each time, from 1,213 to 1,511 to 1,890 mm. After that, rain dropped back to 1,020 mm in 2023, 1,154 mm in 2024 and 1,045 mm in 2025. So the record year was a peak, not the new normal.

points.h: Averaged by decade, the 2020s stand out
points.p: Zooming out, the average year in the 1900s brought 924 mm, and most decades through the 1980s stayed between about 770 and 980 mm. The 1990s rose to **1,036 mm** and the 2010s to **1,055 mm**. The 2020s average **1,306 mm** a year, though this decade is only partly done and includes the record 2022. Still, it is already well above every earlier decade.

story.takeaway: 2022 is Bengaluru's wettest year in the records, and several of the other wettest years are recent. Yet the last few years have been much drier than 2022, so the high average for the 2020s rests heavily on one huge year.
story.note: Each year is the total of its twelve monthly rainfall figures; the 2020s average covers 2020 to 2025 only.
